questions.q: What is new about how MTTD and MTTR are used in Post-Incident Activity, compared to how they were first introduced?
options: They're recorded per-incident and tracked as a trend across similar incidents over time, not calculated once as a single aggregate number
They are renamed to entirely different metrics
They can only be measured once per year
They stop being relevant once an incident is resolved
questions.explain: The metrics themselves are familiar from SOC Operations & SIEM Fundamentals; what's new is tracking them per-incident as a trend.

questions.q: Why does a single incident's MTTR tell you almost nothing on its own?
options: Every incident is different, so one data point can't show whether the team is actually improving — a trend across similar incidents is needed
MTTR is not a real or valid metric
MTTR can only be measured by external auditors
A single incident's MTTR is always exactly the same number
questions.explain: A downward trend across several similar incidents is what provides real evidence of improvement, not one number alone.

questions.q: In the business email compromise trend example, what specifically improved MTTR between incident one and incident two?
options: Jordan's access fix and Priya's playbook change meant the MFA check that used to take an hour now took under five minutes
The attacker used a completely different, easier-to-detect technique
The SOC hired three new analysts
The incident was misclassified as lower severity
questions.explain: The specific action items from Lesson 2's after-action report directly produced the faster MFA check in the second incident.

questions.q: Besides checking whether MTTD/MTTR trended down, what else does this lesson say must be verified?
options: Whether the after-action report's action items were actually completed by their named owners and deadlines
Whether the incident made local news coverage
Whether the SIEM vendor contract needs renewal
Whether the attacker was ever criminally prosecuted
questions.explain: Trend data shows whether things got faster, but checking action items confirms the team actually did what it said it would do.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe Chapter 6 as a whole, once all four lessons are put together?
options: A complete feedback loop: a meeting surfaces issues, a report assigns owned fixes, a Sentinel rule makes one permanent, and measurement confirms it worked
A one-time paperwork exercise with no real operational effect
A replacement for the entire NIST incident response lifecycle
A step that only applies to incidents involving email
questions.explain: Chapter 6 works through the full Preparation-to-Preparation cycle from Chapter 1, now backed by real evidence.
